title: API 570 Training in Philadelphia: Piping Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 570 exam prep for Philadelphia-area piping inspectors: refinery units, chilled NGL lines, traced asphalt piping and CUI, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 570 Training in Philadelphia: Online Exam Prep for Process Piping Inspectors at Delaware Valley Refineries, Gas-Liquids Plants and Terminals
html:
API 570 exam prep for Delaware Valley piping inspectors

In a refinery or gas-liquids plant there is far more pipe than vessel, and most of the API 570 work around Philadelphia is spread along the river: unit piping at Trainer, Paulsboro and Delaware City, chilled lines at Marcus Hook, and transfer lines between docks and tank farms on both banks. This page is for the UT technicians who take the readings, the inspectors who set the circuits and intervals, and the engineers and pipefitters who want API 570 certification.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia. You study the API 570 course online at your own pace, sending questions to an instructor whenever a B31.3 calculation or an API 570 clause will not come clear. API, through its Individual Certification Programs, sets the eligibility rules, runs the examination at Prometric test centres and certifies those who pass; finishing the course is preparation, not certification, and Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

The piping circuits behind the refinery numbers

EIA’s 2026 Refinery Capacity Report shows three operating refineries in the Philadelphia area, and its downstream columns hint at where each one’s piping workload sits (figures in barrels per stream day unless noted):

  • Monroe Energy, Trainer. Hydrotreating of 80,000 for naphtha, 34,000 for gasoline, 23,300 for kerosene and jet fuel and 53,300 for diesel. Delta Air Lines bought the refinery in 2012 to make jet fuel, and said then that the plant’s output, with product exchanges, was expected to provide 80 percent of its US jet fuel needs. Hydrogen-rich feed and effluent lines, sour water and wash water are where much of the inspection effort goes on units like these.
  • PBF, Delaware City. A fluid coker of 54,500, a catalytic cracker of 82,000 fresh feed, 65 million cubic feet a day of hydrogen production and 596 short tons a day of sulfur. Catalyst and coke-handling lines bring erosion; hydrogen and the sulfur plant bring high-pressure hydrogen piping, amine and sour water circuits.
  • PBF, Paulsboro. No catalytic cracker is listed, but asphalt and road oil production of 21,000 and lubricants of 12,000 are. PBF calls Paulsboro the largest asphalt producer on the East Coast, and asphalt means heated, traced and insulated piping that runs hot for long periods.

The practical lesson for a candidate is that circuits and corrosion loops are drawn around process chemistry. An inspector who can explain why a particular feed-effluent line, amine circuit or traced asphalt run is grouped the way it is will find the API 570 sections on inspection planning and CMLs easier to read.

Chilled lines at Marcus Hook

At the Pennsylvania-Delaware line, Energy Transfer’s Marcus Hook complex took its first propane in 2015, according to the company fact sheet DEP posted in 2023, and at the time of that sheet was shipping about 70,000 barrels a day of propane and ethane to local, regional and international markets. The same sheet describes an ethane truck-loading rack commissioned to complement the existing propane terminal and, depending on the season, about 200 trucks a day collecting propane. Behind those numbers sit chilled and refrigerated lines, a splitter and a fractionator, loading headers and a great deal of small-bore pipe.

Cold service changes what a piping inspector looks for. Thinning from the inside is seldom the main threat in dry light hydrocarbons; the threats are on the outside and in the metal. Insulation on a chilled line has to keep moisture out, and where a vapour barrier fails, water condenses and freezes under the jacket. Lines that run cold and then sit at ambient during idle periods cycle through the conditions that make corrosion under insulation worst, which API 570 and API RP 583 treat as a priority. Carbon steel that can be driven below its minimum design metal temperature during depressurisation needs brittle fracture screening, and small-bore branches near pumps and truck racks need checks for vibration fatigue.

Heated lines: asphalt, lubes and the city’s chemical terminal

The opposite problem sits upriver, in the city. Kinder Morgan’s Philadelphia terminal on North Delaware Avenue lists product heating, nitrogen blanketing, vapour recovery and incineration, and steaming of tank trucks and tank cars among its services for chemicals and ethanol, and PhilaPort’s Tioga liquid bulk berth next door connects with that tank farm. Across the river, PBF describes the idle CPI refinery site at Paulsboro as marine, railcar, asphalt and storage infrastructure. Heated product means steam or electric tracing, and traced lines are some of the hardest in any plant to keep dry: steam leaks wet the insulation from inside, tracing hides the pipe surface, and the operating temperature may sit in the band where corrosion under insulation is fastest.

Read the CUI paragraphs of API 570 for what they ask an inspector to do, not for numbers to memorise: identify the susceptible systems, inspect where the insulation is damaged or the water gets in, and decide how much insulation to remove using the owner’s experience and the code’s guidance. The exam asks about the method; the Delaware Valley gives you plenty of places to practise it.

Freeze, thaw and a tidal river

Philadelphia’s weather is hard on insulated pipe. The National Weather Service normals for Philadelphia International Airport list a January normal low of 26°F and a July normal high of 87.8°F, so jacketing seals open and close through the year, condensation forms on cool lines in humid summers, and trapped water freezes and splits stagnant branches in winter. Dead legs, drains and instrument connections that hold water are the obvious places to look after a hard freeze.

The river adds chloride. The Delaware River Basin Commission says the salt front averages around Wilmington and that salty water can corrode industrial intakes and other infrastructure, so cooling-water piping drawing from the lower river, especially below Wilmington, carries a pitting and fouling load that fresh-water plants upstream do not. Dock lines, pipe racks close to the water and soil-to-air interfaces at piers and berths complete the external picture.

Worked example: a chilled propane line whose CML readings hid a CUI pit

A 4-inch Schedule 40 carbon steel line carries chilled propane at a gas-liquids terminal. It has vapour-barrier jacketing and spends part of each year idle at ambient temperature. The owner gives its required thickness, the greater of the pressure design thickness and the structural minimum, as 0.120 in. Its one CML is read through an inspection port: 0.237 in. ten years ago, 0.231 in. five years ago and 0.234 in. today.

  1. Read the trend before you calculate. The long-term rate is (0.237 − 0.234) ÷ 10 = 0.0003 in. a year. The short-term figure suggests the wall grew by 0.003 in., which it cannot have done; that is measurement scatter from probe position, temperature or couplant, and it should be questioned, not entered as a negative rate.
  2. Look where the water gets in. An external visual inspection finds torn jacketing at a support shoe a few feet from the CML. With the insulation removed, the pipe there is pitted, and pit-depth and UT measurements put the deepest remaining wall at 0.150 in.
  3. Estimate a local rate. If the line went into service 16 years ago at 0.237 in., the average pit rate is (0.237 − 0.150) ÷ 16 = about 0.0054 in. a year. CUI usually starts only after the coating breaks down, so the true active rate is likely higher than this average.
  4. Set the next measurement. Remaining life at the pit is (0.150 − 0.120) ÷ 0.0054 = about 5.5 years, so half of it is under 3 years, and never more than the class maximum for the line. In practice the owner repairs the coating and insulation, and decides on the pipe, well before then.

The CML was telling the truth about the pipe beneath intact insulation; it said nothing about the support shoe. That is the point API 570 makes when it separates thickness monitoring from CUI inspection, and it is the reasoning an exam scenario about insulated piping is testing. The API 570 practice questions page has more rate and interval drills.

Where API 570 meets the docks, racks and pipelines

Gas liquids reach Marcus Hook through the Mariner East pipelines from western Pennsylvania, and cross-country lines like these are regulated as pipelines, with their own federal safety rules and pipeline codes, rather than as API 570 process piping. A piping inspector meets them at the plant boundary, where the owner’s documents decide which valve belongs to which regime.

Terminal piping is more often treated as plant piping. Kinder Morgan’s Philadelphia terminal lists two docks on the Delaware, one for ships and one for barges, and the transfer lines from them to the tank farm are the kind of above-ground, insulated and bare carbon steel runs that many owners manage under API 570. Idle terminals add their own questions: Energy Transfer’s Fort Mifflin terminal in Tinicum Township, which formerly received crude oil at two river docks, took its last shipment in June 2019 and is inactive, according to a DEP permit fact sheet from early 2025. How piping is laid up, monitored while idle and inspected before it carries product again is a judgement an API 570 inspector should be able to defend.

From Philadelphia piping jobs to API 570 eligibility

API counts experience gained within the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. Local candidates usually arrive from one of these jobs:

  • UT and CML technicians. Contract technicians who take thickness readings on Delaware Valley units are performing inspection activities. A two-year technical degree means two years of experience, a high-school diploma three. Atlantis offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training for Philadelphia, including UT, for anyone still building the method side.
  • Pipefitters. Union pipefitters, such as members of Philadelphia’s Steamfitters Local 420, can build toward API 570 through piping construction and repair work, which counts on the longer routes as long as at least one year was spent supervising or performing inspection.
  • Operators. Operating experience with piping systems counts on the same longer routes, provided the year of inspection is part of it.
  • Engineers. A BS in engineering or technology needs one year of supervising or performing piping inspection as API 570 describes it, the shortest route.
  • Welding inspectors. B31.3 and Section IX questions will feel familiar; Atlantis also runs AWS CWI exam prep in Philadelphia.

API verifies the experience, not Atlantis. The API 570 certification requirements page sets out each route.

Keeping B31.3 and API 570 moving through a Delaware Valley year

Outdoor work around Philadelphia tends to bunch into the warmer months, so the self-paced format helps most when you plan around it: cover API 570, RP 574 and the damage mechanisms in RP 571 during the quieter winter weeks, then switch to B31.3 navigation and timed papers as your window approaches. B31.3 is long, and most open-book time is lost finding the right table rather than doing the arithmetic, so practise locating allowable stresses, weld joint factors and the pressure design formula in the PDF until you can do it quickly. Keep a list of the circuits you meet at work and ask the instructor how the code would treat each one.

Apply to API before your chosen window’s deadline and study the editions on its Publications Effectivity Sheet, not the ones on your site’s bookshelf. API 570 is taken in person, and Prometric lists test centres in and around Philadelphia.

Sponsoring a piping inspection group from a Philadelphia-area site

Terminal operators, refineries and inspection contractors often want several piping inspectors certified at once. One enquiry can cover a group spread across Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware, and each person studies on their own timetable. Fees are quoted on request. Every candidate applies to API individually, so check each person’s experience against API’s routes before enrolling them.

faq.q: Can I prepare for API 570 in Philadelphia without travelling to a class?
faq.a: Yes. There is no Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia; the course is online, self-paced and supported by instructor Q&A, so you can study between shifts at Trainer, Marcus Hook or a New Jersey terminal. Only the examination is in person: API administers it at Prometric test centres, and Prometric lists centres in and around Philadelphia.

faq.q: Are the Mariner East pipelines covered by API 570?
faq.a: No. Cross-country lines such as Mariner East are regulated as pipelines under federal pipeline safety rules and are built and maintained to pipeline codes. API 570 is the in-service inspection code for process piping. At a plant like Marcus Hook the owner’s documents define where the pipeline ends and the plant piping begins, and that boundary is worth knowing exactly.

faq.q: Does corrosion under insulation really matter on a refrigerated propane line?
faq.a: Yes, and sometimes more than on warm lines. If the vapour barrier on a chilled line fails, moisture condenses and freezes under the jacket, and lines that cycle between cold operation and ambient temperature spend time in the conditions where CUI is most aggressive. API 570 asks you to find susceptible systems and inspect where insulation is damaged, not only to trend CML readings.

faq.q: Is steam-traced asphalt piping something the API 570 exam asks about?
faq.a: The exam does not ask about a particular site, but it does test corrosion under insulation, damage mechanisms from API RP 571 and inspection practice from RP 574 as listed in your window’s Body of Knowledge. Traced, insulated asphalt and lube lines like those at Paulsboro are good real-world practice for understanding why the code treats CUI as a priority.

faq.q: I take UT readings for a contractor in Delaware County. How close am I to API 570?
faq.a: If your readings are part of piping inspection work under an authorized inspection agency, that is inspection experience. With a high-school diploma you need three years within the last 10, with a two-year technical degree two years, and a BS in engineering or technology one. Keep a record of the units, circuits and tasks you worked on; API reviews and verifies it.

faq.q: Should a Philadelphia inspector take API 570 or API 510 first?
faq.a: Take the one that matches your daily work. Contract inspectors on turnarounds and CML crews usually spend most of their time on piping, so API 570 comes first; owner-user inspectors responsible for columns and exchangers may start with API 510. Many add the second certification later. Atlantis’s comparison of the API certifications sets out the trade-offs.

faq.q: Can a terminal operator enrol inspectors from Pennsylvania and New Jersey together?
faq.a: Yes. One enquiry and one quote can cover inspectors at different sites and in different states, and each person studies at their own pace with instructor Q&A. Fees are quoted on request. The state you work in makes no difference to the API examination, which every candidate applies for and sits individually.
